summary: Gives a corrected description of the control commands exchanged between Network Control Programs to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol of RFC 123. It fixes an error in RFC 127 pointed out by Eric Harslem of Rand. It was replaced by RFC 165.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 145 gives a corrected table of the NCP commands used to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 123. It shows how the server and user establish their connections and allocate messages and bits.

subtitle: A corrected listing of NCP commands for the Initial Connection Protocol.

tldr.problem: An earlier listing of the Network Control Program commands for the Initial Connection Protocol contained an error.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 145 gives the server and user NCP command exchange, including the initial 32-bit transfer and the later connections used for data flow.
tldr.outcome: RFC 145 obsoletes RFC 127, was later obsoleted by RFC 165, and was updated by RFC 143.

sections.title: A Corrected Initial-Connection Exchange
sections.content:
Jon Postel presents an interpretation of the Network Control Program (NCP) exchange needed to carry out the Initial Connection Protocol in RFC 123. He says this note corrects an error pointed out by Eric Harslem of RAND.

RFC 145's header says it obsoletes RFC 127.
sections.plainLanguage: This note corrects an earlier table of the NCP messages used to establish an initial connection.

sections.title: The Command Sequence
sections.content:
The server listens on link L while the user sends RTS, U, L, l_A. The server replies with STR, L, U, 32; the user sends ALL, l_A, 1, 32. The server sends 32 bits in one message, and the user receives the value S.

Both NCPs then send CLS. They establish further links using STR and RTS commands that include the value S, wait for the connections, and send ALL commands for message and bit allocations. The table then shows data flowing on the new links.
sections.plainLanguage: The peers first establish a link to exchange 32 bits, then close it. They use the received value to establish further links for data.

sections.title: Link and Allocation Notation
sections.content: The symbols l_A, l_B, and l_C represent links; m_B and m_C represent message allocations; and b_B and b_C represent bit allocations. The remaining symbols are defined in RFC 123.
sections.plainLanguage: The small-letter symbols label links and their message or bit allocations. RFC 123 defines the other symbols.
